Article Title: Asian Games Medal Tally: India win 8 medals but remain outside top 10 as gold continues to elude
Article Text:
Yashvir Singh, Rohit Yadav, and Esha Singh

Eight medals, but no gold for India

Shooting and kurash add to India's tally

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Asian Games Medal Tally after Day 9

Rank Nation Gold Silver Bronze Total 1 China 132 53 45 230 2 Japan 41 68 63 172 3 South Korea 21 26 43 90 4 Uzbekistan 12 17 13 42 5 Kazakhstan 9 13 23 45 6 Thailand 9 8 13 30 7 Bahrain 9 2 3 14 8 Iran 8 15 9 32 9 North Korea 7 5 5 17 10 Malaysia 6 3 9 18 11 Hong Kong 5 12 17 34 12 INDIA 4 20 21 45

NEW DELHI: India produced another strong medal haul at the Asian Games 2026 on Monday, winning eight medals across athletics, shooting and kurash. However, the impressive collection did not bring any change in the overall standings, with India remaining 12th as the country continued to wait for another gold medal.India added four silver and four bronze medals during the day but could not increase its gold tally. After Day 9, India stood at 45 medals — four gold, 20 silver and 21 bronze.'The eight-medal haul included silver medals for Yashvir Singh, Murali Sreeshankar, Gulveer Singh and Esha Singh, while Rohit Yadav, Parul Chaudhary, Vithya Ramraj and Pincky Balhara won bronze.India's strongest showing came in the men's javelin, where Yashvir and Rohit produced a double podium finish in the absence of defending champion Neeraj Chopra.Yashvir recorded a personal best of 85.72m for silver, while Rohit won bronze with 84.35m. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage claimed gold with 88.55m.Sreeshankar also won silver in the men's long jump with 8.07m despite an injury forcing him to abandon his final two attempts. China's Yuhao Shi took gold with 8.17m.Gulveer added his second silver of the Games with a personal best of 3:36.72 in the men's 1500m, having earlier finished runner-up in the 10,000m.Parul Chaudhary won bronze in the women's 5000m with 15:14.61, adding to the bronze she had claimed in the 3000m steeplechase.Vithya Ramraj also took bronze in the women's 400m hurdles with a personal best of 54.75 seconds.Esha Singh secured silver in the women's 25m pistol after finishing with 38 hits, the same score as China's Xiao Jiaruixuan, who won the gold after the shoot-off.Pincky Balhara added bronze in the women's -78kg kurash category, losing 0-5 to South Korea's Sumin Mo in the semifinals.Despite the eight medals, India's gold tally remained at four, a crucial factor in the standings as countries are ranked by gold medals first.China led with 132 golds, followed by Japan with 41, South Korea with 21 and Uzbekistan with 12. India remained 12th with 45 medals, highlighting how a large haul of silver and bronze medals has yet to translate into a significant rise in the standings.
Article Summary: India added four silver and four bronze medals during the day but could not increase its gold tally. China led with 132 golds, followed by japan with 41, south korea with 21 and uzbekistan with 12. India remained 12th with 45 medals, highlighting how a large haul of silver and bronze medals has yet to translate into a significant rise in the standings.

Article Title: “When they’re really in awe of the world”: Jason Kelce opens up on how fatherhood changed his life as he remains inspired by his love for Travis Kelce
Article Text:
Jason Kelce opens up.(Image via Getty Images)

Jason Kelce reflects on fatherhood and how a lot of it is inspired by the bond he has had with Travis Kelce

Jason Kelce’s bond with Travis Kelce remains precious as he always stands by his younger brother’s side

Jason Kelce, the former Philadelphia Eagles’ star player, has always been a present father to the four children he has with his wife, Kylie Kelce. While after retiring from the league, Jason Kelce keeps himself busy with his career as a sports analyst in ESPN and an entrepreneur, the former NFL star has reflected on fatherhood.In an appearance on a podcast, the former Philadelphia Eagles’ star player opened up about it as he said, "Every little thing she kinda picks up on, and she's starting to go out of that age a little bit, but that's my favorite stage — when they're really in awe of the world, and they wanna talk about everything…”Jason Kelce added, “And, things that you take for granted on a really regular basis are put more in the forefront of your mind." You get to experience the world again through the lens of, like, a tiny human who's just doing it for the first time."In another interaction, Jason Kelce’s wife, Kylie Kelce, also opened up about their daughters as she said, "I'm two for two. Way to go, Ellie. Ellie made it out of preschool without getting kicked out like her father and her uncle…”Jason Kelce’s wife Kylie Kelce joked, “I really do think the true test is going to be two years from now when Benny gets to hit that threshold, if she makes it there.And that's the key."She continued, "Wyatt loved kindergarten…I think Ellie is also going to love kindergarten, but I do think that it is going to be a little eye-opening for her because she is not quite into academics in the same way that Wyatt is."Ever since the former NFL star Jason Kelce tied the knot with Kylie Kelce, the two have been focused on building a family together.In the last few years, Jason Kelce and his wife, Kylie Kelce, have become parents to four daughters and have always tried to keep them out of the spotlight.While the former Philadelphia Eagles’ star Jason Kelce has always been a present father, he has often spoken about how a lot of it is inspired from the bond he has with the Kansas City Chiefs’ tight end, Travis Kelce.Both Jason Kelce and Travis Kelce have been pretty close and have always stood by each other’s side.Today, both of them have started multiple businesses together as Travis Kelce remains a star player in the Kansas City Chiefs.
Article Summary: Jason kelce has always been a present father to the four children he has with his wife, kylie kelce. The former philadelphia eagles’ star player has often spoken about how a lot of it is inspired from the bond he has had with the kansas city chiefs’ tight end, travis kelcie.

Article Title: Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes’ $325 million KC Current opens new doors for UMKC women’s soccer players
Article Text:
Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes (Instagram)

Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes’ KC Current partnership

KC Current and UMKC build a pathway beyond soccer

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes’ investment in the KC Current is creating an impact that reaches well beyond professional soccer. Through the club’s partnership with the University of Missouri-Kansas City, members of the women’s soccer team recently gained direct access to professional players and the lessons that come with life at the highest level. The mentorship session with KC Current player Haley Hopkins gave the Roos a chance to ask honest questions about pressure, confidence, training and life after college. For student-athletes balancing academics with competition, the experience offered something a classroom cannot easily provide: a closer look at what it takes to build a career in sport.The KC Current has become an important part of Kansas City’s growing women’s sports scene. Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes are among the club’s ownership group, giving the Chiefs power couple a direct connection to an organisation that continues to invest in women’s soccer.That connection is now helping create opportunities for the next generation. The UMKC partnership brings professional experience closer to student-athletes, allowing players to learn from athletes who have already faced many of the challenges they are navigating.Hopkins spoke about her path from youth soccer and college competition to the National Women’s Soccer League. Her advice focused on practical issues such as preparation, confidence and managing life away from the pitch.For senior health sciences major Maddie Muhr, the experience carried lessons that will last longer than a season.“I feel lucky to have this opportunity,” Muhr said. “I haven’t heard of any other program that gets to be so closely tied with another amazing program like the KC Current. It’s amazing to see the strides they make on and off the field and being able to meet them and grow alongside them is super cool.”The value of the partnership extends beyond technical training. Players heard about resilience, discipline and the reality of preparing for life after college sport.Muhr said those lessons stood out because they apply far beyond soccer.“Regular training is showing up, getting your work done,” she said. “But when players come here and talk to us, they are teaching us life lessons that go beyond the field, beyond the game and training, and that is what’s really going to stick with you after college. College is such a short time, and what I learned today is really going to be valuable post-college and in life in general.”UMKC senior and former student-athlete Audrey Brown also highlighted the value of hearing directly from professionals.“There are ups and downs, but these Current players always push through,” Brown said. “Their story really inspired me.”UMKC deputy athletic director Ursula Gurney said professional mentors can give student-athletes perspectives that extend beyond university life.The KC Current’s connection with UMKC shows how professional sports ownership can have an impact beyond games and business. With Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes part of the club’s ownership group, the partnership reflects a broader investment in Kansas City’s women’s sports community and the young athletes who hope to shape its future.
Article Summary: Patrick mahomes and brittany mahomes’ investment in the kc current is creating an impact that reaches well beyond professional soccer. Through the club’s partnership with the university of missouri-kansas city, players gained direct access to professional players.

Article Title: Travis and Jason Kelce quietly donated $10,000 to help turn a $50,000 Olympic fundraiser into a family reunion in Milan
Article Text:
Travis and Jason Kelce (Instagram)

Travis and Jason Kelce helped Laila Edwards’ family reach Milan

Travis Kelce supported Laila Edwards before Olympic gold

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Earlier this year, Travis and Jason Kelce made a quiet contribution that helped make a special Olympic moment possible for U.S. hockey star Laila Edwards. The brothers donated $10,000 to a fundraiser that helped bring Edwards’ family and friends to Milan for the 2026 Winter Olympics. Their support came after her family faced a difficult choice between watching her Olympic debut and covering everyday household expenses. Edwards went on to help Team USA win gold, creating a moment her family could celebrate together.Edwards’ Olympic journey was already historic before she stepped onto the ice. The 22-year-old became the first Black American to win an Olympic medal in women’s ice hockey after Team USA defeated Canada in the gold-medal game.But getting her loved ones to Italy was not easy.Edwards’ father, Robert Edwards, launched a GoFundMe campaign titled “Send Laila’s Family to the Olympics to Cheer Her On!” with a $50,000 target. The goal was designed to help the family avoid choosing between Olympic travel and essential bills at home in Cleveland Heights, Ohio.The Kelce brothers, who also grew up in Cleveland Heights, had followed Edwards’ career since she became the first Black player to make the U.S.senior women’s national team in 2023. They later supported her through an anonymous $10,000 donation.The contribution helped make the trip possible for 14 people, including Edwards’ parents, grandmother, aunt, cousin and older brother.The family had initially been able to afford travel for only two people.“We had to start talking about how to get money,” her mother Charone Gray-Edwards said, according to the Associated Press. “Who would go? How would we afford it?”The Chiefs tight end’s support extended beyond the financial contribution. Travis also reached out to Edwards before her Olympic debut, offering encouragement as she prepared for the biggest stage of her young career.“He was just saying, everyone’s got my back. He’s rooting for me,” she said, per the AP. “They didn’t have to do that, but they did. And I’m really grateful.”Jason Kelce and his wife, Kylie, were also in the stands for the gold-medal game, giving Edwards a familiar connection to her hometown while she represented the United States.Edwards made an impact on the ice, recording an assist during the gold-medal victory. Team USA eventually defeated Canada 2-1 in overtime, securing only the third Olympic gold medal in U.S. women’s hockey history.For Edwards, the victory was more than a sporting achievement. Her family had made the long journey to Milan, and the Kelce brothers had quietly helped make that possible. Their involvement added another meaningful layer to an already historic Olympic chapter.
Article Summary: Travis and jason kelce donated $10,000 to a fundraiser that helped bring laila edwards' family and friends to milan for the 2026 winter olympics. Their support came after her family faced a difficult choice between watching her olympic debut and covering everyday household expenses. Edwards went on to help team usa win gold.

Article Title: Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez’s £89,000 charity helped a 7-year-old receive treatment for rare type of cancer
Article Text:
Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez (Credit: Getty Images)

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez supported Tomas’ cancer treatment

Cristiano Ronaldo’s charity work extends beyond cancer support

In 2021, Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez were reported to have quietly stepped in to help a seven-year-old Portuguese boy battling a rare form of cancer. Tomas had been diagnosed with neuroblastoma in September 2019 and faced another setback after the disease returned. As his family searched for financial support for further treatment, a message shared by Georgina’s sister appeared to confirm that the football star and his partner had contributed. Their reported gesture added to a long record of charitable work that has included support for hospitals, children’s organisations and humanitarian causes.Tomas’ situation had become increasingly difficult after his cancer relapsed in October 2020. His parents appealed for help as they tried to secure the treatment their young son needed.The boy later travelled to Barcelona, where he was admitted to D’Hebron Hospital for tests and consultations with oncology specialists. His case had also attracted attention from people across Portugal, who rallied around the family during a stressful period.The reported involvement of Ronaldo and Rodriguez emerged through a message shared by Georgina’s sister, Ivana.Rather than announcing the contribution themselves, the couple were thanked publicly for helping Tomas access treatment.The message included a direct expression of gratitude:“Thank you Georgina and Cristiano for your help, solidarity and great heart.“Infinite thanks for helping us so that Tomas can access treatment.”The wording indicated how important the support was to Tomas’ family as they worked to continue his medical care.Ronaldo has previously used his profile and resources to support humanitarian causes. His charitable record includes both direct donations and work with major international organisations.During the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, Ronaldo and his agent, Jorge Mendes, donated £1 million to support hospitals in Portugal as healthcare systems faced intense pressure from the virus. The contribution was directed towards hospitals in Lisbon and Porto, according to reports at the time.Ronaldo has also served as an ambassador for organisations including Save the Children, UNICEF and World Vision. In another notable gesture, he donated his £89,000 UEFA Team of the Year bonus to the Red Cross in 2013.For Tomas and his family, however, the focus was much closer to home. The reported support from Ronaldo and Rodriguez came at a critical point in the child’s treatment journey. Their contribution was part of a wider effort by people who wanted to help the young boy continue receiving specialist care.The episode also showed how private acts of generosity can become public when families need support and choose to acknowledge those who helped them during a difficult time.
Article Summary: Cristiano ronaldo and georgina rodriguez were reported to have quietly stepped in to help a seven-year-old portuguese boy battling a rare form of cancer. Tomas had been diagnosed with neuroblastoma in september 2019 and faced another setback after the disease returned.

Article Title: 86 to 101: Virat Kohli's final ODI window to break Sachin Tendulkar's century record
Article Text:
Virat Kohli's final ODI window to break Sachin Tendulkar's century record

86 to 101: The century equation begins

India or overseas? The recent pattern in Kohli's centuries

2027 World Cup: Kohli's final shot at Sachin's record

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Only ODI cricket remains

It was the semi-final of the 2023 World Cup when Virat Kohli scored his 50th ODI century in front of Sachin Tendulkar, surpassing his idol's record of 49 hundreds in the format. That innings put another Tendulkar record within Kohli's reach. Tendulkar's 100 international centuries remain the benchmark, leaving Kohli with a chance to become the first batter to reach 101.But the equation changed when Kohli retired from Test cricket on May 12, 2025. With his T20I career already over, ODI cricket became his only remaining route to Tendulkar's record. Now, with the 2027 World Cup less than a year away, Kohli has 86 international centuries - 14 short of equalling Tendulkar and 15 away from surpassing him.His latest hundred, a 139 not out against West Indies in the first ODI of the recently concluded series, was followed by 29 in the second match and a golden duck in the third.So how many opportunities does Kohli have left, and can he turn them into the 15 centuries he needs to move past Tendulkar's 100?India currently have 11 confirmed bilateral ODIs scheduled before the 2027 World Cup - five against New Zealand, three against Sri Lanka and three against Zimbabwe.India's World Cup campaign will begin against Australia in Cape Town on October 7, 2027.The new FTP could add another six-match ODI series in South Africa in the weeks before the World Cup, giving India a chance to acclimatise to conditions ahead of the tournament. However, that series is not part of the confirmed schedule as of yet.The Asia Cup is another part of the picture. The 2027 tournament is scheduled to be played in Bangladesh from June 18 to July 4 and is expected to return to the ODI format. A detailed fixture list has not been announced, but based on the 2023 format, India could play up to six matches if they reach the final.The World Cup itself will have five group-stage matches and if the team reaches the Super 7, they will play six more matches, with a semi-final and final to follow if they go all the way. A finalist could therefore play a maximum of 13 matches at the tournament.That leaves Kohli with 11 confirmed bilateral ODIs before the World Cup, with the Asia Cup providing additional opportunities before the tournament.For Kohli, the target remains 15 centuries.Kohli's recent ODI numbers are markedly different at home and overseas. In his last 32 ODI matches in India, he has scored nine centuries. In his last 32 overseas ODIs, he has scored three - in Dubai, Chattogram and Colombo.That split comes into focus with India scheduled to play five ODIs in New Zealand before the World Cup.Kohli's overall record overseas, though, is substantial. He has scored 27 of his 55 ODI centuries outside India. Bangladesh is his most productive overseas country, with six centuries, followed by Sri Lanka and Australia with five each. He has four in the West Indies, three in South Africa and one each in New Zealand, England, Zimbabwe and the UAE.Sri Lanka remains one of Kohli's most productive opponents. Kohli has scored 10 ODI centuries against Sri Lanka, his highest tally against any opponent. The three-match series in December will be played in India, with the ODIs scheduled for December 13, 16 and 19. Zimbabwe follow with three matches on January 3, 6 and 9.Kohli's World Cup record gives him a strong base to build on. In 37 World Cup matches, he has scored 1,795 runs at an average of 59.83, with five centuries and 12 half-centuries.The 2023 edition was his most productive World Cup. He scored 765 runs, including three centuries and six half-centuries, and finished as the tournament's leading run-scorer. It was also the tournament in which he scored his 50th ODI century, moving past Tendulkar's record of 49.Kohli has already crossed 15000 ODI runs, becoming only the second batter after Tendulkar to reach the mark. He did so in his 303rd innings. With Test and T20I cricket behind him, every international century Kohli scores from here will come in ODIs. He has also said that the 2027 World Cup will be his last World Cup for India.Fifteen hundreds remain between Kohli and 101.
Article Summary: Virat kohli has scored 86 odi centuries, 14 short of sachin tendulkar's record. The 2027 world cup is less than a year away. India have 11 confirmed bilateral odis before the world cup. Kohli is 15 away from surpassing his idol's 100 international centuries. Kohli scored 765 runs, including three centuries and six half-centuries.

Article Title: 'I feel I have done my duty': Harmanpreet Kaur steps down as India captain
Article Text:
Harmanpreet Kaur (BC​CI Photo)

HARMANPREET KAUR STATEMENT:

Today, I step down as captain of the Indian Women’s Cricket Team across all formats.

This is not an easy decision. It carries years of memories, emotions, sacrifices, and moments that will stay with me for the rest of my life.

I have given everything I had to this team and to Indian women’s cricket — my blood, my sweat, my time, and many times, a part of my own game and personal ambitions. There were moments when I had to put my individual performance, my own growth, and what I wanted for myself aside, because I believed the team had to come first.

As a captain, I have had to make difficult decisions.

Decisions that were not always understood, not always easy, and sometimes came at a personal cost. But every decision I made was with one intention - to make this TEAM better and to give other players the opportunity to grow, believe in themselves and become the best versions of themselves.

I have seen it all.

I have seen the lowest moments, the heartbreak, the criticism, the doubts and the days when nothing seemed to go our way.

And I have also experienced the highest highs - the victories, the celebrations, the pride of representing our country, and the moments that made every sacrifice worth it.

NEW DELHI: Lovlina Borgohain ’s Asian Games gold was not just a medal upgrade from silver in the last edition. It was the latest marker in a 15-year career that has taken the Assam boxer through Olympic success, injuries, difficult phases and a mentally demanding Paris 2024 campaign.At the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Borgohain finally changed the colour of her Asian Games medal, defeating China’s Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the women’s 75kg final. The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second Indian woman after MC Mary Kom to win boxing gold at the Asian Games -- 12 years after Kom’s 2014 triumph.For Borgohain, however, the gold's significance went beyond the history books.“It’s still difficult to get out of this moment. I still have the gold medal in my hand," said a beaming Borgohain while lifting the gold medal next to her face. "It’s a very special moment for me. I can’t express how I feel,” she continued as she spoke to TimesofIndia.com upon returning from Japan.Borgohain had finished with silver at the 2022 Hangzhou Asian Games, losing to China’s Li Qian in the final. Three years later, she returned to the continental stage determined to go one step further.Her path to the gold in Nagoya was not straightforward. She began with a 5-0 quarter-final win over South Korea’s Seong Su-yeon before edging Kazakhstan’s reigning 70kg world champion Natalya Bogdanova 3-2 in a closely fought semi-final.She then produced a 5-0 win over Ziyi in the final.The contrast with Hangzhou made the medal particularly meaningful.“Every event is very important. We believe that the Asian Games medal is the highest after the Olympics. I think this medal is shining amidst all the medals. The colour has changed. This medal means a lot to me,” Borgohain said.“I got a silver medal in the last Asian Games and this time I got a gold medal. This is why it is so special. And to do it on my birthday is extra special.”The victory also continued a curious connection between Borgohain and Japan. Five years ago, Tokyo had brought her an Olympic bronze medal — the breakthrough that changed the trajectory of her career.“I was very excited because I was going to Japan again. I had won a medal in (the) 2020 Olympics in Japan, and my life changed because of that,” she said.“I had a positive mindset before leaving India. I wanted to make it the best tournament of my life. I knew that I could do it because Japan is lucky for me.”The gold also offered a reminder of Borgohain’s ability to rebuild.Her career has not followed a straight line since the Tokyo Olympics. Injuries, changes in form and the disappointment of the Paris Olympics tested her, while the pressure that came with becoming an Olympic medallist added another layer to the challenge.Borgohain does not, however, see the Asian Games gold as something that has fundamentally changed her.“I don’t think I am looking at myself differently because of this medal. I have won and lost a lot of medals. People’s perspective changes because of the medal. But I am always the same in my own eyes,” she said.“My perspective has not changed because of the medal. When I lose, my self-belief remains the same. Sometimes I am confident, and sometimes I am down. But I am the same person that I was before.”That mindset became particularly important after Paris 2024, when she failed to reach the medal rounds. Borgohain describes the period as one of the most difficult phases of her career.“I have a 15-year journey. Every time I go to a competition, my mindset is different. When we play, we reach the medal. It is not easy to recover from a tough period. The 2024 Paris Olympics wasn’t an easy period for me mentally,” she said.“But I think everything is a game of the mind. It depends on how we look at it. If we take tough things easy, it becomes easy. If we take easy things hard, it becomes hard. I think that helped me a lot to keep myself calm and relaxed.”The Asian Games victory has also given Borgohain a more direct route towards the next stage of her career. The gold means she qualifies for the World Championships, rather than having to go through the national selection route. A strong performance there could also put her on the road to another Olympic qualification campaign.“It matters a lot for an athlete because of this medal I am qualifying for the World Championships. I am getting a good treat otherwise I would have to play the Nationals and follow the same process,” she said.“So that is a big advantage of the medal, and it boosts my confidence that I can do better. If I do well there, then I can qualify for the Olympics also.”For now, though, Borgohain is resisting the temptation to look too far ahead.“There is a lot of planning. But not everything is the same. I am living in the present. I don’t know what will happen tomorrow. I will try to live like this. It makes me feel good. I will try to live like this.”Borgohain’s gold was part of a strong boxing campaign for India at the Asian Games. India finished the competition with six boxing medals, including three golds, with Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal also winning their respective finals.Some months back, Indian boxers had returned with 10 medals at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, including seven golds. No country had won more golds in boxing at a single edition of the CWG. It was also India's largest haul in the sport in a CWG.For Borgohain, the improvement reflects a broader change in the mentality of Indian boxers.“We had a very good performance. Both men and women did very well. Everyone knows the results of the Commonwealth Games. The results of the Commonwealth Games changed the results of Indian Boxing,” she said.“In the Asian Games, our Indian team came out on top. I think our athletes are very strong. Their mentality is very good. We used to think that we would not be able to do it. But now our young athletes have the mindset that ‘we have to do it’.”She also pointed to the support structure around the team, including government backing and the environment created by the coaching staff led by Santiago Nieva.“The support of the government matters a lot. They don’t let us down. We are getting good competition. The environment of our foreign coaches, led by Santiago (Nieva), is very positive. That is why we are getting good results.”For Borgohain, then, the Asian Games gold is both an ending and a beginning — the end of a 12-year wait since Mary Kom’s historic gold and the completion of a personal journey from Hangzhou silver to Nagoya gold.But she is not treating it as a destination. The next target can wait. For now, she is content to live in the moment — with the gold medal still in her hand.

The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second indian woman after mc mary kom to win boxing gold at the asian games -- 12 years after kom’s 2014 triumph. Article Title: 'Captaincy ends': Harmanpreet Kaur’s top five achievements as India captain

A legacy that goes beyond the numbers

NEW DELHI: Harmanpreet Kaur ’s decision to step down as captain of the Indian women’s cricket team across all three formats marks the end of one of the longest and most significant leadership eras in Indian women’s cricket.The 37-year-old, who led India’s T20I side for a decade after taking over in 2016, became the ODI captain in 2022 before taking charge across formats in 2023. On Tuesday, she announced that she was ready to move on from leadership and return to playing simply “for the love of the game”.“Captaincy ends. The journey continues,” Harmanpreet wrote in her farewell statement.Her tenure was defined by landmark victories, records and moments that helped shape the modern era of Indian women’s cricket.From finally winning the ODI World Cup to establishing herself among the most successful captains in T20I history, Harmanpreet leaves behind a remarkable leadership legacy.Here are the five biggest achievements of Harmanpreet Kaur’s captaincy stint.The biggest achievement of Harmanpreet Kaur’s captaincy was undoubtedly India’s historic triumph in the Women’s ODI World Cup in November 2025.For decades, an ODI World Cup title had remained one of the biggest missing pieces in Indian women’s cricket.India had come agonisingly close before, finishing runners-up in 2005 and 2017, but the trophy continued to elude the team.That changed under Harmanpreet.Leading India on home soil, she oversaw the campaign that finally delivered the country its first-ever Women’s ODI World Cup title. The achievement carried enormous significance not only for Harmanpreet personally but also for the growth and visibility of women’s cricket in India.The triumph represented the culmination of years of progress. India had developed into a consistent force in international cricket, producing a generation of players capable of competing with the world's best. Harmanpreet's leadership was central to that transition.Winning a World Cup as captain is the defining achievement of any international cricketer. For Harmanpreet, doing so with the Indian women's team made the moment even more significant.The title also ensured that her captaincy legacy would be remembered for more than individual records. She became the leader who helped India cross the final barrier and turn years of promise into a world championship.Another significant achievement of Harmanpreet Kaur’s captaincy was leading India to gold medals at consecutive Asian Games, reinforcing the team’s dominance in the T20 format on the continental stage.India won the women’s cricket gold medal at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, where cricket made its return to the Games after a long absence. Harmanpreet’s side emerged victorious in the T20 competition, securing India’s first-ever Asian Games gold in women’s cricket.India then successfully defended its title at the 2026 Asian Games, once again finishing at the top of the women’s T20 competition. The back-to-back triumphs highlighted the consistency of the Indian team under Harmanpreet’s leadership and added another pair of major medals to her captaincy résumé.Winning one Asian Games gold was a landmark achievement. Repeating that success four years later demonstrated that India had established itself as the dominant force in the continental competition.Another defining feature of Harmanpreet's captaincy has been India's dominance in the continental game.Under her leadership, India secured four Asia Cup titles, in 2012, 2016, 2022 and 2026, giving Harmanpreet the distinction of being the Indian captain with the most Asia Cup triumphs.The Asia Cup has traditionally been an important tournament for women's cricket in the region, providing teams with an opportunity to test themselves against familiar opponents while also developing younger players.For India, success in the competition has reflected the team's sustained strength.Harmanpreet's four titles also demonstrate the longevity of her leadership. The fact that her successful campaigns stretched across more than a decade is particularly notable. Different teams, different opponents and different generations of Indian players came and went, but Harmanpreet remained a constant presence.The achievement saw her surpass Mithali Raj for the most Asia Cup titles by an Indian captain.That places Harmanpreet in distinguished company. Mithali was one of the central figures of Indian women's cricket for more than two decades, and succeeding her in the record books is a significant marker of Harmanpreet's own influence.The 2026 title was especially important because it came near the end of her captaincy tenure, providing another continental trophy to close one of the most successful leadership chapters in Indian women's cricket.Harmanpreet Kaur’s impact was perhaps most pronounced in T20I cricket, where she spent a decade at the helm after taking over as India’s captain in 2016. Her remarkable longevity not only made her one of the longest-serving leaders in women’s international cricket but also saw her establish several historic records.One of her biggest achievements came when she surpassed Australia’s Meg Lanning to become the captain with the most wins in women’s T20 internationals. The record reflects the consistency and longevity of Harmanpreet’s leadership at a time when the shortest format was undergoing rapid growth around the world.Her T20I tenure also produced another extraordinary milestone. Harmanpreet became the first cricketer in history to captain a side in 150 T20I matches, underlining the remarkable length of her leadership career.Reaching that landmark required far more than simply holding the captaincy. It reflected sustained selection, fitness, performance and, crucially, the confidence of teammates and coaches over many years. During her tenure, women's cricket witnessed the rise of franchise leagues, increasingly demanding international schedules and major tactical developments in T20 cricket.While Harmanpreet's greatest achievements have largely come in limited-overs cricket, one of her most memorable leadership moments arrived in the longest format.She guided India to a dominant 270-run victory over England at Lord's, in the first women's Test match played at the historic London venue.Lord's is one of the most iconic grounds in world cricket, and playing there carries enormous significance regardless of format. For the women's game, the occasion was historic in its own right.India's victory made the event even more memorable.A Test match places very different demands on a captain compared with T20 cricket. Leaders must manage sessions rather than individual overs, balance workloads across multiple days and constantly assess pitch conditions, field placements and bowling changes.Harmanpreet's ability to guide India to a comprehensive victory demonstrated her adaptability as a leader.The 270-run margin also highlighted India's superiority during the match. It was not merely a narrow escape or a hard-fought result; it was a commanding performance at one of cricket's most famous venues.For Harmanpreet, the achievement added another dimension to her captaincy record.Harmanpreet Kaur's decision to step down brings an era to a close, but her contribution to Indian women's cricket will extend far beyond captaincy statistics.She led India through a period of enormous change, from the rapid growth of T20 cricket to the expansion of women's franchise leagues and the eventual breakthrough of a World Cup triumph.Her five standout achievements, the 2025 ODI World Cup, the T20I captaincy wins record, four Asia Cup titles, the 150-match leadership milestone and the historic Lord's Test victory, encapsulate the scale of her tenure.Yet perhaps the most telling part of her farewell was her belief that the team is now “in a good place”.Harmanpreet is stepping away from the leadership role, but not from the game. As she put it, she is now ready to play for the love of cricket again.The captaincy may have ended. The journey, however, continues.
Article Summary: Harmanpreet kaur's decision to step down marks the end of one of the longest and most significant leadership eras in indian women's cricket. The 37-year-old led india’s t20i side for a decade after taking over in 2016. She became the odi captain in 2022 before taking charge across formats in 2023.

India’s medal-winning campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 has reached 80 medals, with the contingent winning 18 gold, 26 silver and 36 bronze medals. India are currently fifth in the overall medal standings.India’s medal tally received a major boost over the last two days, with the contingent adding gold medals across boxing, wrestling, archery, hockey and golf. Lovlina Borgohain, Parveen Hooda, Ankush Panghal, Sujeet Kalkal, the Indian women’s hockey team, Kumkum Mohod and Pranavi Urs have all contributed gold medals to India’s latest surge.Kumkum also won silver alongside Dhiraj Bommadevara in the mixed recurve team event, while India’s women’s golf team of Pranavi Urs, Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar secured silver.On October 3, Kumkum Mohod added another gold by winning the women’s individual recurve event. The 17-year-old defeated South Korea’s Oh Yejin 6-5 in a shoot-off to become the first Indian woman to win an individual recurve medal at the Asian Games. Her victory also secured an Olympic quota place for India for the 2028 Los Angeles Games.Pranavi Urs also scripted history by becoming the first Indian woman to win individual golf gold at the Asian Games, while helping India claim silver in the women’s team event alongside Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar.India’s women’s cricket team won the country’s first gold medal of the Games after defeating Sri Lanka in the final. Suruchi Singh and Kamaljeet then added India’s second gold by winning the 10m air pistol mixed team event.India subsequently won both the men’s and women’s kabaddi titles, while Neeru Dhanda secured gold in the women’s trap event. She later teamed up with Kynan Chenai to win the mixed trap team gold.In athletics, Kiran Pahal, Poovamma Machettira, Prachi Choudhary and Vithya Ramraj won gold in the women’s 4x400m relay. India also dominated the compound archery events, winning gold in the men’s team, women’s team and mixed team events.On October 2, Lovlina Borgohain defeated China’s Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the women’s 75kg final to win gold. The victory came on her birthday and made Lovlina only the second Indian woman boxer after Mary Kom to win an Asian Games gold.The women’s recurve team of Ankita Bhakat, Kirti Sharma and Kumkum Mohod then created history by defeating South Korea 5-3 to win India’s first-ever Asian Games gold in the event.India then added three more gold medals in boxing and wrestling, with Parveen Hooda winning the women’s 65kg title, Ankush Panghal taking gold in the men’s 80kg category and Sujeet Kalkal winning the men’s freestyle 65kg event.The Indian women’s hockey team ended a 44-year wait for Asian Games gold by defeating China 1-0 in the final, with the victory also securing a direct qualification spot for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.On October 3, Kumkum completed a memorable Asian Games campaign by winning individual recurve gold. After being pushed to a shoot-off by Oh Yejin, the 17-year-old held her nerve to shoot a 10 and beat the South Korean 8, securing India’s first individual women’s recurve gold at the Asian Games.Pranavi Urs added another historic gold in golf. The 23-year-old became the first Indian woman to win an individual golf gold medal at the Asian Games. She also helped India win silver in the women’s team event.India’s silver medal haul has come across shooting, athletics, weightlifting, wushu, squash, wrestling, sailing, archery and golf.The shooting contingent has been one of India’s biggest contributors, with medals across air rifle, 50m rifle 3 positions, 25m pistol and trap events.Mirabai Chanu ended her long wait for an Asian Games medal by taking silver in the women’s 49kg weightlifting event, while Roshibina Devi won silver in women’s 60kg sanda. Gulveer Singh also enjoyed a strong Games, winning silver in the men’s 10,000m and 1500m events.In squash, Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh won silver in the women’s and men’s singles events respectively. India also collected silver medals in sailing and archery, with Prince Noble Kurisinkal and Manu Francis finishing second in the men’s skiff.Kumkum Mohod and Dhiraj Bommadevara lost to China in the mixed recurve final, while Dhiraj Bommadevara, Neeraj Chauhan and Yashdeep Bhoge finished runners-up to South Korea in the men’s recurve team event.The latest addition came in golf, where Pranavi Urs, Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar won silver in the women’s team event. China took gold, while India finished second.India’s bronze medals have come from a wide range of disciplines, including shooting, athletics, squash, boxing, wrestling, archery, sailing, sepaktakraw, badminton, rowing, table tennis, kurash, soft tennis and mixed martial arts.Athletics has produced a large share of India’s bronze medals, with Parul Chaudhary, Gulveer Singh, Tejaswin Shankar, Vithya Ramraj, Pooja Singh, Rohit Yadav and others contributing to the tally.India’s squash contingent has also produced multiple medals, with Joshna Chinappa, Velavan Senthilkumar, Anahat Singh, Tanvi Khanna, Abhay Singh and Veer Chotrani contributing across the mixed doubles and team events.In boxing, Narender Berwal, Priya Ghanghas and Kapil Pokhariya won bronze, while Sunil Kumar secured bronze in Greco-Roman wrestling.Nethra Kumanan won bronze in the women’s dinghy sailing event, while India’s men’s quadrant team secured bronze in sepaktakraw after losing 0-2 to Japan in the semifinal.

Article Title: How Adidas's Harry Miles thinks supershoes can reach every runner
Article Text:
Harry Miles, who directs footwear innovation at Adidas, presents the Adizero Sprint Spike Concept at the company's Home of Innovation in Herzogenaurach.

A supershoe's sole purpose is saving energy

The Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3 that Sabastian Sawe wore to run the first official sub-two-hour marathon, signed with his finishing time.

The real engineering is buried in the midsole

The Adizero Adios Pro 5, launched days before the Berlin Marathon, uses the same carbon Energyrim as the Evo 3.

It's a long run from the track to the road

The Adizero Sprint Spike Concept, built for sprinters, on display in Adidas's lab during the Berlin Marathon weekend.

A sprinter settles into the blocks during a demonstration at Adidas's Home of Innovation, where cameras track how an athlete's foot loads and pushes off in the first strides.

The weekend runner is still the hardest customer to design for

The Adizero Evo SL uses Adidas's Lightstrike Pro racing foam without any rods, at a lower price than the brand's plated shoes.

The shoe on the table beside Harry Miles is one almost nobody reading this will ever wear. The Adizero Sprint Spike Concept, one of many concepts Adidas had on show, is made for sprinters who run 100 metres in under 10 seconds, whose feet touch the ground for about a tenth of a second on each stride, under forces several times their body weight.Miles directs footwear innovation at Adidas and has worked on everything from custom shoes for ultramarathon record attempts to football boots, so he knows better than most how far that spike is from the way most people run."You wouldn't take this onto the road if you're doing a 5K jog in the morning," he said at Adidas's Home of Innovation in Herzogenaurach, where the company opened its labs to visitors over the Berlin Marathon weekend.That distance runs through the entire supershoe category. Since carbon-plated racers with high-rebound foams arrived in 2017, every major sportswear brand has built its fastest shoes around the same basic recipe. The word "supershoe" has done a lot of marketing work since then, but underneath it sits a fairly precise piece of engineering.That engineering peaked in April, when Sabastian Sawe ran the first official sub-two-hour marathon in Adidas's Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3, a shoe tuned for someone covering a kilometre in under 2 minutes 50 seconds.Yomif Kejelcha crossed the line 11 seconds behind him in the same shoe. On Sunday in Berlin, the Evo 3 swept both the men's and women's podiums, the first time a single brand has done that at a major marathon since 2017.The Evo 3 also points to where the category is heading. It is designed to last a single marathon, its foam and upper too fragile for much more, and it costs $500 in the US, when you can find one at all. Shoes like it are starting to be called hypershoes, a tier above the supershoes that defined the last decade.That leaves the Adizero Adios Pro 5, launched days before Berlin, as the supershoe tier below the Evo 3. It was on many feet at this year's race, and plenty more runners have had their eyes on it, and then on its eye-watering price.A runner at 6 minutes per kilometre also lands, loads and pushes off shoes like these in a very different way from Sawe. Closing that gap, Miles says, is the point of the work."The most important part of what we do is not only delivering for the few people who are capable of breaking world records, but also making sure it becomes accessible at scale for the masses."How that happens is an engineering question, and his answer starts with what a supershoe is actually for.Ask Miles what a supershoe does and he doesn't talk about speed. He talks about efficiency, and uses an electric car to explain it.A runner starts every race fully charged. The more efficient the system, the less charge it uses at any given pace, so the runner can either go faster for the same effort or reach the final kilometres with something left in the battery. For most people buying these shoes, that is a more honest pitch than speed. Very few of them will ever race anyone but themselves.Sports scientists call this running economy, the oxygen a runner needs to hold a steady pace, and measuring it is about as unglamorous as the field gets. The athlete runs, usually on a treadmill, with a mask strapped to their face while a gas analyser reads every breath. Miles describes the same routine at Adidas: prototypes on athletes' feet, masks on their faces, and the numbers deciding which version survives.Weight is where the easiest gains are. Since the 1980s, researchers have known that every 100 grams added to a shoe raises the energy cost of running by about 1 per cent, because that weight has to be lifted and swung on every stride. Run those numbers across the tens of thousands of steps in a marathon and it is easy to see why the industry has spent four decades shaving grams.The Evo 3 weighs 97 grams, with rubber cut down to a thin layer only where the foot needs grip. Adidas says it is 1.6 per cent more economical than the previous Evo, though that figure comes from the company, not independent testing.A lab session only captures an athlete on one day. The fuller picture comes from training, and this is where AI comes into shoe design.Adidas collects training data through smartwatches and sensors it gives athletes at training camps. Miles says all of it, along with the lab data, ends up in "big machine learning systems" that surface the right insights from the right athletes far faster than before.Anyone who has opened a running watch export will understand why. One session produces continuous readings of stride, ground contact time, cadence and heart rate, and across dozens of athletes and months of training, that becomes far more than any team can compare by hand. Finding patterns in more numbers than anyone has time to read is exactly the kind of job machine learning suits.Miles is careful to call it one tool among many at Adidas, and that restraint makes the claim easier to believe.Strip a racing shoe down and most of its efficiency sits in two parts, the foam and the carbon. These are also the parts Miles expects to reach ordinary runners first, and in Adidas's line-up, some of it already has.A midsole works like a spring. It compresses when the foot lands, stores energy and gives part of it back at push-off. Whatever it doesn't give back is lost as heat inside the material, which engineers call hysteresis.The aim is a foam that loses less energy and weighs less, and Adidas says Lightstrike Pro Evo, the foam in the Evo 3, is around half the weight of the previous version. That previous version, Lightstrike Pro, shows how the trickle-down works.The Adizero Evo SL uses that racing foam on its own, with no rods, in a simple construction, and it costs less than the plated Boston 13. Further down the range, the Adizero SL2 blends Lightstrike Pro with the older Lightstrike 2.0 EVA foam and regularly turns up in sales. Each step down trades a bit of race-day bounce for a lower price and a longer life.That longer life matters. Very light, very bouncy foams tend to wear out sooner than the denser foams in everyday trainers, which makes a supershoe closer to a consumable than a long-term buy. The hyper shoe takes that to its logical end: one race, and done. Anyone who has retired a pair of racers earlier than planned will know the feeling.Carbon's job is less obvious. At push-off, the joints where the toes meet the foot bend, and that bending absorbs energy the runner never gets back. A stiff carbon structure limits the bend and, together with a curved rocker sole, rolls the foot forward. Miles likens getting that stiffness right to picking a gear: too little and the runner is in the wrong one, too much and the gear is set too high to be quick.Brands have approached that stiffness in different ways, from full-length plates to separate carbon rods, and Adidas has just changed its own approach. The Evo 3 drops the traditional plate for a carbon Energyrim, which lets Adidas fit more foam underfoot while staying within World Athletics' limits. The Pro 5 inherits it, replacing the rod-shaped Energyrods of earlier Adios Pro models, and the company says it returns 9 per cent more energy than the previous version.The rods haven't disappeared, though. The Boston 13 borrows the Energyrods from the Adios Pro 4 to add punch to faster training sessions, and Adidas describes the ones in that shoe as glass-fibre Energyrods 2.0, tuned for a softer but still propulsive ride. They are a less rigid, less expensive version of the same idea.This is why the spike on the table can't simply be scaled down. A sprinter's foot is on the ground so briefly that the shoe works almost entirely at the forefoot, under loads a jogger never comes close to. A recreational runner's foot stays down more than twice as long and often lands further back, so the foam stiffness, plate shape and rocker all have to be tuned again before any of the thinking carries over. Presenting the concept, Miles put the gap in numbers. Sawe took roughly 20,000 steps to win in London, while Oblique Seville won last year's 100 m world title in fewer than 50, which leaves a spike under a quarter of a per cent of the steps to make its difference.Spike technology has already crossed over once. For its F50+ football boot, Adidas took the stiff plate and lightweight, high-rebound foam from its track spikes and adapted them for footballers, a project Miles co-wrote about for the company. The Sprint Spike Concept, as it happens, borrows the Evo 3's Energyrim and Lightstrike Pro Evo foam, so the traffic already runs both ways. A road shoe is the next and harder crossing, because a jogger's stride is further from a sprinter's than a winger's is.Miles says that is the work Adidas is doing now: looking at how the principles that make a spike fast over 100 metres could become something a person out for an early 5 km on a Sunday can feel. He puts it a few years out, after which this kind of technology becomes, in his words, "more accessible and more usable" for road runners.The Pro 5 shows how that usually plays out. It carries Evo 3 technology at a price that still keeps it out of reach for many, and for most runners the benefit only arrives once it trickles down again into trainers like the Evo SL and the Boston.The hyper shoe may speed that up. Every time the ceiling moves higher, what used to sit at the top moves down a tier. The foams and carbon that defined race day a few years ago now turn up in trainers with entry-level price tags across brands, and the Evo SL is Adidas's version of that. For everyday runners, a $500 shoe that lasts one race is less a product to buy than a preview of what their next pair might carry.How quickly that happens depends on how fast the company learns. One of the slowest parts of building a shoe, Miles says, has always been the wait between testing a prototype with an athlete and having data worth acting on.At three months per prototype, a team gets about four attempts a year. At one month, it gets roughly twelve, each tested and refined before the design is locked."If you close the loop much quicker, you can learn faster," he says, sounding more like a software engineer than a shoe designer. It is also the most convincing case in the conversation for how elite technology gets fast-tracked to the rest of us.Taken far enough, that loop could close around a single foot. Almost every shoe today is built on a last, a standard foot-shaped mould, with the same foam density running through the midsole, which means it is designed for an average foot that nobody actually has.Earlier in the day at Adidas's APEX Lab, I had seen what the alternative looks like: shoes 3D printed for individual athletes. The printer is the part everyone photographs, but the more interesting work happens before it starts. A foot scan and motion capture map where an athlete's foot takes the most pressure, where it flexes and how force moves through it on every stride, and the shoe is built around that map instead of an average. Every new session sharpens the map for the next pair, which is Miles's loop at its most personal. For now, only a handful of athletes get to wear one.The further a runner is from that handful, the less certain the science gets. Independent research on everyday runners is still unsettled. Some studies find the economy gain narrows at slower paces, with a few runners measuring worse in the shoes, while others find it holds.Part of the problem is that there is no such thing as a typical weekend runner. An elite field sits in a narrow band of bodyweights, cadences and foot strikes, and Adidas can fit a shoe to each athlete in it. The runners behind them at a city marathon range from heel strikers to forefoot runners and from 50 kg to 100 kg, often on roads far rougher than a closed race course. They need one shoe that works for all of them, lasts hundreds of kilometres and costs a fraction of a racer. That is a harder brief than a world record.The maths does have a quirk that favours slower runners. Someone on the course for four and a half hours gains more minutes from the same percentage improvement than someone finishing in just over two, so a small efficiency gain means more to them, not less.So what does a sub-two-hour marathon change for someone running 5 km on a Sunday? Not much right away. Super shoes at the very top, or hypershoes as the likes of the Evo 3 are now being called, will stay rare and expensive. Over the next few years, though, what was learned building them will filter down, first into shoes like the Pro 5 and then into more affordable trainers such as the Adizero Evo SL, Boston and SL2. That slow trickle, more than any record, is what Miles means when he talks about reaching the masses.Whether any of it ever shows up on a recreational runner's watch is still an open question. The more likely payoff is one the watch won't record at all: a run that leaves a little more in the legs, in a shoe that carries a little of what was built for the front of the race.
Article Summary: Adidas opened its labs to visitors over the berlin marathon weekend. The adizero sprint spike concept is made for sprinters who run 100 metres in under 10 seconds. Shoes like it are starting to be called hypershoes, a tier above the supershoes. The evo 3 weighs 97 grams, with rubber cut down to a thin layer only where the foot needs grip.
